faq.a: Yes. Requests above 272K input tokens are billed at 2x the input and cache rates and 1.5x the output rate, so $4.00 in and $15.00 out, applied to the whole request rather than only the excess tokens.

paras: $1.00 per 1M input tokens and $5.00 per 1M output tokens, with cache hits at $0.05 — five percent of the uncached rate. Cache writes are the only number that surprises people: $1.25 per 1M for 30-minute retention and $2.50 for 12-hour retention, so a workload that rewrites its prefix every turn pays for the writes it never reads.

The model sits exactly halfway between GPT-6.1 Sol and nothing: Sol costs $2/$10, so Terra is half on both sides, and GPT-6 Astra costs $10/$50, so Terra is a tenth. For the same 1.05M context window and the same 128K maximum output, that is the widest price gap OpenAI has put between two tiers with identical context limits.

sections.h2: The 272K cliff is the number to watch
paras: Terra inherits the same long-context rule as Astra and Sol: a request above 272K input tokens is billed at 2x the input and cache rates and 1.5x the output rate, and the multiplier applies to the entire request, not just the tokens past the threshold. A 400K-token prompt with 20K of output costs $0.95 instead of $0.50, which means the cost of crossing the line is 90% of the request, not 32% of it.

In practice that makes chunking cheaper than long context below roughly 272K, and it makes 300K-token requests the most expensive mistake on this price list. Measure prompt length before you assume the headline rate.

sections.h2: Why the per-token price understates the shift
paras: OpenAI's own numbers put GPT-6.1 Terra at 57.6% on Agents' Last Exam at medium reasoning effort, against 42.6% for GPT-5.6 Terra, at $0.29 per task versus $0.84. A 15-point accuracy gain and a 65% cost cut at the same time is the reason this tier matters: the constraint on always-on agents was never capability, it was whether you could afford to let them run.

Treat vendor benchmarks as directional. The 50.3% Terminal-Bench 4.0 figure at maximum reasoning effort still means half of those tasks go unsolved, and every headline number here comes from the vendor's own harness.

faq.q: How much does GPT-6.1 Terra cost per 1M tokens?
faq.a: $1.00 per 1M input tokens and $5.00 per 1M output tokens. Cached input bills at $0.05 per 1M, and cache writes cost $1.25 per 1M for 30-minute retention or $2.50 for 12-hour retention.

faq.q: Is GPT-6.1 Terra cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol?
faq.a: Yes, by exactly half: $1.00/$5.00 against Sol's $2.00/$10.00, with the same 1.05M context window and 128K maximum output. Sol is the tier for complex coding and long-horizon reasoning; Terra is the tier for high-volume computer use, visual reasoning and writing.

faq.q: What happens above 272K input tokens?
faq.a: The whole request is repriced at 2x input and cache rates and 1.5x output: $2.00 in, $0.10 cached in, $7.50 out. The multiplier applies to every token in the request, so a 300K-token prompt costs more than twice what the same prompt costs at 270K.

faq.q: Does GPT-6.1 Terra have a batch discount?
faq.a: Yes. Batch and Flex processing cost 50% of standard ($0.50/$2.50), and Fast mode costs 2x standard. The long-context multiplier stacks on top of whichever mode you pick.

faq.q: What is GPT-6.1 Terra's context window and knowledge cutoff?
faq.a: 1,050,000 tokens of context and 128,000 maximum output tokens, with a knowledge cutoff of 1 June 2026. Reasoning effort can be set to none, low, medium, high, xhigh or max, and medium is the default.

sections.h2: What DeepSeek V4.1 Flash actually costs in October 2026
paras: $0.15 per 1M input and $0.60 per 1M output are off-peak rates. DeepSeek bills double during two weekday windows, 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC, which cover seven hours a day, five days a week — about 21% of the calendar. Weekends and Chinese public holidays bill off-peak all day, so roughly 79% of the week sits at the rates on this page.

Cache hits cost $0.003 per 1M tokens, fifty times cheaper than a miss at $0.15. For an agent that resends the same system prompt most of the input never pays the full rate: the worked example below runs at $2.33 a month instead of $6.30.

The 1017 snapshot, released 2026-10-17, kept the price and cut output length by roughly 30%. Cost per finished task fell without a rate change, which is why per-token price is a poor proxy for cost per outcome.

sections.h2: V4.1 Flash or V4 Pro: when the cheap tier is enough
paras: Flash is 4.4x cheaper on input and 3.3x cheaper on output than V4 Pro, and it wins on two things besides price: it accepts images, which Pro rejects, and it allows 2,500 concurrent requests against Pro's 500. For extraction, classification, vision and high-volume fan-out there is no reason to pay the premium.

Where Pro earns its price is long-horizon reasoning. If a wrong answer costs more than the tokens, the cheaper model is the expensive choice — the 3.7x gap on the cached loop above is worth paying when a retry chain costs an hour of engineering time.

faq.q: How much does DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost per 1M tokens?
faq.a: $0.15 per 1M input tokens and $0.60 per 1M output tokens at off-peak rates. Weekday peak (01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC) doubles both, to $0.30 and $1.20. Cached input bills at $0.003 per 1M.

faq.q: Is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cheaper at night?
faq.a: Yes. Off-peak rates are half the peak rates. Peak covers seven hours per weekday, so about 79% of the week bills at the lower rate; weekends and Chinese public holidays are off-peak all day.

faq.q: Should I use V4.1 Flash or V4 Pro?
faq.a: Flash for extraction, classification, image input and high-concurrency work: it is 4.4x cheaper on input and 3.3x cheaper on output, accepts images, and allows 2,500 concurrent requests against 500. Use V4 Pro when reasoning depth is worth the premium.

faq.q: Does DeepSeek V4.1 Flash accept image input?
faq.a: Yes. Flash is multimodal while V4 Pro is text-only, which is often the deciding difference for document, screenshot and chart workloads.

faq.q: What changed in the 1017 snapshot?
faq.a: Same price, but outputs run about 30% shorter, so cost per completed task dropped. The model name is deepseek-flash; the retired deepseek-v4-flash aliases are served by this snapshot and billed at the Flash price.

sections.h2: What DeepSeek V4 Pro actually costs in October 2026
paras: $0.66 per 1M tokens is the off-peak rate, not the list price. DeepSeek publishes peak rates and halves them outside two weekday windows: 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC. That is seven hours a day, five days a week, about 21% of the calendar. The other 79% bills at the rates above, and Chinese public holidays count as off-peak all day.

Cache hits are the widest lever here. A cache hit costs $0.022 per 1M tokens against $0.66 for a miss, a 30x difference. An agent that resends the same long system prompt pays full price for it once and almost nothing afterwards, which is why the worked example below drops from $25.74 to $8.51 a month.

There is no batch-API discount for this model. DeepSeek does not publish one, so the 50% asynchronous saving that OpenAI, Anthropic and Google offer has no equivalent here. Time-of-day pricing replaces it, and it is worth the same 50% if your jobs can wait for an off-peak window.

sections.h2: V4 Pro or V4.1 Flash: what the price gap buys
paras: V4 Pro costs 4.4x more on input and 3.3x more on output than V4.1 Flash. Two non-price differences decide the call: V4 Pro is text-only while Flash accepts images, and V4 Pro's concurrency limit is 500 against Flash's 2,500, which matters when you fan out hundreds of parallel requests.

Route by task shape rather than by model rank. Extraction, classification, image input and short chat belong on Flash; long-horizon reasoning where a wrong answer is expensive justifies Pro. Sending every request to Pro at 4.4x the input rate is rarely the right default.

sections.h2: The hidden cost: Search and Fetch billing starts 1 November 2026
paras: DeepSeek bills its Search and Fetch APIs per request at $0.75 per 1,000 successful calls, and those calls are free until 00:00 Beijing time on 1 November 2026. From that date retrieval becomes a separate line item, so a search-heavy agent pays twice: once for tokens and once for lookups.

Worked example: five search calls per turn, 20 turns a day, is 3,000 calls a month, or $2.25. That is about 26% on top of the $8.51 token bill above. For retrieval-heavy workloads the search line can exceed inference, and no token calculator will show it.

faq.q: How much does DeepSeek V4 Pro cost per 1M tokens?
faq.a: $0.66 per 1M input tokens and $1.98 per 1M output tokens at off-peak rates. Weekday peak (01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC) doubles both, to $1.32 and $3.96. Cached input bills at $0.022 per 1M.

faq.q: Is DeepSeek V4 Pro cheaper at night?
faq.a: Yes. Off-peak rates are half the peak rates. Peak covers seven hours per weekday, so about 79% of the week bills at the lower rate; weekends and Chinese public holidays are off-peak all day.

faq.q: Does DeepSeek V4 Pro have a batch API discount?
faq.a: No. DeepSeek does not publish a batch discount for this model, so the 50% asynchronous saving offered by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google has no equivalent here. Off-peak pricing and cache hits are the available levers.

faq.q: Should I use V4 Pro or V4.1 Flash?
faq.a: Flash for extraction, classification, image input and high-concurrency fan-out: it is 4.4x cheaper on input and 3.3x cheaper on output, accepts images, and allows 2,500 concurrent requests against 500. Use V4 Pro when reasoning depth is worth the premium.

faq.q: What does DeepSeek charge for Search and Fetch?
faq.a: $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests, free until 00:00 Beijing time on 1 November 2026. After that, retrieval is billed separately from tokens and can add around 26% to a search-heavy agent's bill.

sections.h2: What Kimi K3.1 Pro costs, and what it is cheaper than
paras: $2.00 per 1M input tokens and $10.00 per 1M output tokens, with cache hits at $0.20. That is a third below Kimi K3 at $3/$15, and a fifth of GPT-6 Astra at $10/$50, which is the comparison Moonshot itself leads with.

The rate card is flat: unlike OpenAI, Google and xAI, Moonshot does not reprice long prompts, so the full 1,048,576-token window bills at the same per-token rate as a 1,000-token request. That single fact is the reason to look here for document work — a 400K-token prompt on this model costs $0.80 of input, while the same prompt on GPT-6.1 Terra costs $0.80 before the long-context multiplier and $1.60 after it.
Cache writes are billed by TTL and are not refunded: $2.00 per 1M for 5-minute retention, $4.00 for an hour. Short-lived prefixes should stay on the default 5-minute TTL.

sections.h2: Highspeed: the same model at twice the price
paras: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is not a different model. It serves the same weights with 2-3x the output speed and bills $4/$20 with $4/$8 cache writes, so the decision is purely whether latency is worth 100% more per token. Interactive products usually say yes; batch pipelines almost never do.

Both variants require a minimum $1 top-up to unlock, and both keep thinking mode on permanently with reasoning effort limited to low, high or max. There is no way to turn reasoning off, which matters when you are pricing a chat workload with short answers — every reply carries hidden thinking tokens billed at the output rate.

faq.q: How much does Kimi K3.1 Pro cost per 1M tokens?
faq.a: $2.00 per 1M input tokens and $10.00 per 1M output tokens, with cached input at $0.20 per 1M. Cache writes cost $2.00 per 1M for 5-minute retention and $4.00 for one hour.

faq.q: Does Kimi K3.1 Pro charge more for long context?
faq.a: No. Moonshot bills a single flat rate across the full 1,048,576-token context window, with no long-context multiplier. That makes it cheaper than OpenAI and Google tiers for prompts above roughly 272K tokens, where those providers reprice the whole request.

faq.q: Kimi K3.1 Pro or K3.1 Pro Highspeed?
faq.a: Same weights, same 1M context, same $0.20 cache hits. Highspeed outputs 2-3x faster and costs $4.00/$20.00 with $4.00/$8.00 cache writes. Choose it when latency is user-visible; stay on standard for batch work.

faq.q: Is Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights?
faq.a: Yes, at 3T-class parameter scale — the largest open-weight model published so far, by Moonshot's account. Full weights are scheduled for release by 4 November 2026; the API is available now.

models.name: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
models.note: Released 2026-10-19. Half the M3 rate on input and output and 70% cheaper cache reads, with 428B total / 23B active parameters, open weights and roughly 200 tokens per second

paras: $0.15 per 1M input tokens, $0.60 per 1M output tokens and $0.015 per 1M cached input — a flat rate across the 1M-token window, with no long-context multiplier published. Against MiniMax M3 at $0.30/$1.20 that is half price on both sides and a 75% cut on cache reads.

On the numbers this is the cheapest credible agent tier in this table: $0.60 output undercuts DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's $0.60 only on paper, because DeepSeek's published rate is an off-peak rate that doubles for seven hours every weekday. M3.1 Flash has no time-of-day pricing, so the rate above is the rate you pay at 10am on a Tuesday.

At 23B active parameters out of 428B total, this is a sparse model built for throughput rather than depth — MiniMax quotes roughly 200 tokens per second and a 70% drop in the cost of completing an agentic task, which is a claim about retries and turn count, not about per-token price. A model that needs fewer steps to finish is cheaper than its rate card suggests; one that needs more is more expensive.

Treat the vendor benchmark wins as directional and the independent leaderboard position as the useful signal. For extraction, classification, tool routing and high-volume fan-out this tier is now hard to argue against on price; for long-horizon reasoning the $2-$10 tier still earns its cost.

faq.q: How much does MiniMax M3.1 Flash cost per 1M tokens?
faq.a: $0.15 per 1M input tokens and $0.60 per 1M output tokens, with cached input at $0.015 per 1M. MiniMax's rate card lists a single price across the 1M-token context window.

faq.q: Is MiniMax M3.1 Flash cheaper than MiniMax M3?
faq.a: Yes. Input and output are both half of M3's $0.30/$1.20, and the cache-read rate falls from $0.06 to $0.015 per 1M. M3.1 Flash also removes M3's higher tier for prompts above 512K tokens.

faq.q: Does MiniMax M3.1 Flash have time-of-day pricing?
faq.a: No. Unlike DeepSeek, MiniMax bills the same rate around the clock, so there is no off-peak window to schedule batch work into and no peak multiplier to budget for.

faq.q: Is MiniMax M3.1 Flash open weights?
faq.a: Yes. The weights were released under an open licence on 23 October 2026, four days after the API launch, at 428B total and 23B active parameters.
